content.title: This submission is an extension of proximal-sgd for nonconvex nonsmooth composite optimization. Both theory and experiments are a bit weak.
content.review:
This manuscript considers solving a special class of nonconvex composite optimization via adaptive gradient methods, in which the function is the summation of a nonconvex smooth loss and nonconvex-nonsmooth regularizer which allows easily computable proximal mapping.  Convergence to the stationary point (to be more precise, Frechet subdifferential containing the zero vector) is proved. Empirical studies on training sparse and binary neural network seems to justify its effectiveness. The comparison of the proposed ProxGen and Prox-SGD is also considered. I have following comments. 

1. The update in line 8 of Algorithm 1 requires a closed form of proximal mapping w.r.t. a potentially nonconvex nonsmooth regularizer. Although it holds for some examples (\ell_0 regularization, SCAD, MCP, etc.), It is hard to hold in general. This assumption is a bit strong.
2. It is not immediately clear to me what the technical challenge of proving the convergence in Corollary 1. From my perspective, the proof is adapted from (Xu et al. 2019) and (Chen et al. 2019), in which (Xu et al. 2019) considered solving the same class of problems using Prox-SGD, while (Chen et al. 2019) considered solving nonconvex smooth problems using adaptive gradient methods.
3. It is not shown in theory that the proposed Prox-Gen is better than Prox-SGD in (Xu et al. 2019).
4. The large minibatch requirement in Corollary 1 is not practical for deep learning applications.
5. Assumption (C-3) (i) is kind of weird. Why is it a reasonable assumption?

Experiments:
1. In the experiment of training binary neural network, why the baseline of Prox-SGD is not compared?
2. Only CIFAR10 experiment is reported. It would be desired to see the results on ImageNet, since ImageNet is usually used as a benchmark dataset in quantization literature.
content.rating: 4: Ok but not good enough - rejection
content.confidence: 5: The reviewer is absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct and very familiar with the relevant literature

content.title: Response to Reviewer 2 [1]
content.comment:
Dear Reviewer 2,

Thank you for your constructive feedback

[Q1: The update in line 8 of Algorithm 1 requires a closed-form of proximal mapping. This assumption is a bit strong.]

Actually, the closed-form of proximal mappings is not mandatory, so we make no assumptions on the closed-form in our paper. However, it could be computationally prohibitive if the closed-form of proximal mappings does not exist (for example, the packages for the proximal Newton methods such as glmnet and QUIC performs inexact proximal evaluation for solving quadratic subproblem). For this reason, we consider the regularizers that have closed-form in Section 2 and our experiments.

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[Q2: It is not immediately clear to me what the technical challenges of proving the convergence in Corollary 1.]

Our proofs basically follow the overall arguments in [1], but the details are quite different. Since the existence of momentums and preconditioners in our proof, the distance we should bound $\mathrm{dist}(0, \widehat{\partial}F(\theta_{t+1}))$ of ProxGen is totally different from that of the previous work [1]. Hence, we have to bound the quantity different from what the previous work [1] should bound. In this process, the main challenge is to handle the momentum term and the preconditioner properly, we successfully bypass these difficulties by mild assumptions on the momentums and preconditioners, the condition (C-3) (iii) and (C-4) respectively.

The proof in [2] for solving unregularized non-convex smooth problems is absolutely different from ours. Rather, our Theorem 1 with empty regularizer $\mathcal{R}(\cdot) = 0$ and batch size $m_t = t$ could recover the exactly the same convergence rate in [2] (for example, Corollary 3.1 and 3.2 in [2]).

[1] Non-asymptotic Analysis of Stochastic Methods for Non-Smooth Non-Convex Regularized Problems, Xu et al., NeurIPS 2019.

[2] On the Convergence of a Class of Adam-type Algorithms in Non-convex Optimization, Chen et al., ICLR 2019.

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[Q3: It is not shown in theory that the proposed ProxGen is better than Prox-SGD in (Xu et al. 2019).]

Please see the global response.

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[Q4: The large minibatch requirement in Corollary 1 is not practical for deep learning applications.]

As we stated in Corollary 1, the minibatch size $\Theta(T)$ is the same as $\Theta(\sqrt{n})$ where $n$ is the sample size. The MNIST dataset has $\sqrt{n} = \sqrt{60000} \approx 244$ and ImageNet dataset satisfies $\sqrt{n} \approx 1000$, which we believe are all practical. 

We will also include additional corollary for the increasing minibatch size $b_t = t$ in the revision.

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[Q5: Assumption (C-3) (i) is kind of weird. Why is it a reasonable assumption?]

In other words, the condition (C-3) (i) says that the change of $\theta_t$ at each iteration should be finite. This assumes a regular optimization trajectory excluding an unexpected blow-up case in a single iteration, which we believe is reasonable.

Also, this condition is studied in many previous literatures such as [1,2,3,4].

[1] Adam: A Method for Stochastic Optimization, D.P. Kingma and Jimmy Ba, ICLR 2015.

[2] On the Convergence of Adam and Beyond, Reddi et al., ICLR 2018.

[3] Adaptive Methods for Non-convex Optimization, Zaheer et al., NeurIPS 2018.

[4] On the Convergence of a Class of Adam-type Algorithms in Non-convex Optimization, Chen et al., ICLR 2019.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

content.title: Response to Reviewer 2 [2]
content.comment:
[Q6: In training binary neural networks, why is the baseline of Prox-SGD not compared?]

The purpose of this experiment is to demonstrate our revised ProxQuant since the original update rule in [1] does not consider the preconditioner in their proximal update as we noted in Section 2. Hence, we consider only ProxQuant as a baseline, but the comparison with [2] would be also meaningful.

[1] ProxQuant: Quantized Neural Networks via Proximal Operators, Bai et al., ICLR 2019.

[2] Non-asymptotic Analysis of Stochastic Methods for Non-Smooth Non-Convex Regularized Problems, Xu et al., NeurIPS 2019.

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[Q7: Only CIFAR-10 experiment is reported. It would be desired to see the results on ImageNet in quantization.]

We agree with the reviewer’s opinion that training networks on ImageNet is a standard benchmark in quantization literature. However, the purpose of our work is not to achieve state-of-the-art performance on the quantization, so we consider the largest task considered in [1] to facilitate comparison with [1].

Nevertheless, as the reviewer’s suggestion, we plan to include experiments on ImageNet in later revision.

[1] ProxQuant: Quantized Neural Networks via Proximal Operators, Bai et al. ICLR 2019.

display_title: The authors oversell the content a little bit.

content.title: The authors oversell the content a little bit.
content.review:
This paper oversells a bit. This paper combines the ideas of momentum and the proximal regularized quasi-newton method. The analysis of this method relies on the Lipschitz gradient assumption and the objective function is even assumed to be Lipschitz continuous (C-3) (ii). These conditions are unlikely to be satisfied in the neural network setting. However, it seems to me that the title and the introduction say that the algorithm is tailored for deep learning. This is of course not the case, though it is possible to apply this algorithm heuristically to the training of deep learning. As for the algorithm, the only difference is to involve the momentum term compared to Stephen Becker et al., ‘On Quasi-Newton Forward-Backward Splitting: Proximal Calculus and Convergence’.  

The regularizer can not be an arbitrary lsc function, once you choose Frechet subdifferential for analysis. The Frechet subdifferential \partial f(x) can be empty, say f(x) = -|x| at x = 0.

I do not understand the last paragraph on page 5. The approximate Hessian Ct and the regularization parameter \delta is set by users, it is doable to set this matrix to be positive definite. Why do you need to verify it for a specific application? Whatever the application is, this matrix should be the same since it is chosen by the users. 

I think in Corollary 1, it should be 1/\sqrt{T}.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 4
content.comment:
Dear Reviewer 4,

Thank you for your constructive feedback.

[Q1: The analysis of this method relies on the Lipschitz gradient assumption and the objective function is even assumed to be Lipschitz continuous (C-3) (ii). These conditions are unlikely to be satisfied in the neural network setting.]

As the reviewer said, a neural network does not satisfy the $L$-smooth condition and Lipschitz continuous condition in general. However, these conditions are very standard in convergence analysis of algorithms designed for training deep models, e.g. [1,2,3,4,5] and many other studies.

In our work, our goal is to provide a unified analysis on stochastic proximal methods under standard conditions in non-convex optimization. In this sense, the condition (C-4) is the only additional one, which can be satisfied easily both in theory (see Appendix D) and practice (see Figure 1 in our paper).

[1] Adam: A Method for Stochastic Optimization, D.P. Kingma and Jimmy Ba, ICLR 2015.

[2] On the Convergence of Adam and Beyond, Reddi et al., ICLR 2018.

[3] Adaptive Methods for Non-convex Optimization, Zaheer et al., NeurIPS 2018.

[4] On the Convergence of a Class of Adam-type Algorithms in Non-convex Optimization, Chen et al., ICLR 2019.

[5] Closing the Generalization Gap of Adaptive Gradient Methods in Training Deep Neural Networks, Chen et al., IJCAI 2020.

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[Q2: As for the algorithm, the only difference is to involve the momentum term compared to Stephen Becker et al., “On Quasi-Newton Forward-Backward Splitting: Proximal Calculus and Convergence”.]

In terms of algorithms, the main difference is that our ProxGen considers the “stochastic” PGD with  momentum whereas [1] deals with “deterministic” optimization (i.e., uses full-batch gradient) without momentum.

Moreover, in terms of theory, [1] considers strongly convex loss with convex regularizers while ProxGen guarantees the convergence in a more general setting: a non-convex loss and a non-convex regularizer.

We would like to emphasize that ProxGen is quite different from [1] both in algorithm and theory. Also, our ProxGen framework includes [1] as a special case.

[1] On Quasi-Newton Forward-Backward Splitting: Proximal Calculus and Convergence, Stephen Becker et al., SIAM 2018.

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[Q3: The regularizer can not be an arbitrary LSC function.]

The regularizer should be positive and the Frechet subdifferential should exist. We will modify this in the revision.

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------




[Q4: I do not understand the last paragraph on page 5.]

Since the condition (C-4) says that the minimum eigenvalue of $\alpha_t (C_t + \delta I)^{-1}$ should be lower-bounded by some strictly positive constant $\gamma$ uniformly over the total iteration T. If the minimum eigenvalue shows decreasing behavior as training progresses, such $\gamma$ might not exist. 

However, as in Figure 1, the minimum eigenvalue of $\alpha_t (C_t + \delta I)^{-1}$ tends to increase, so the condition (C-4) holds in practice.

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[Q5: In Corollary 1, it should be 1/\sqrt{T}.] 

In Corollary 1, $O(1/T)$ is correct as we stated since the convergence bound is for the square of the distance.

content.title: Official Blind Review #3
content.review:
Summary: 
The authors studied the training of regularized neural networks where the regularizer can be non-smooth and non-convex. They proposed a unified framework for stochastic proximal gradient descent, PROXGEN, that allows for arbitrary positive preconditioners and lower semi-continuous regularizers. The authors presented the first proximal version of ADAM and a revised version of PROXQUANT. They also analyzed the convergence of PROXGEN and show that the whole framework enjoys the same convergence rate as stochastic proximal gradient descent without preconditioners.  


Comments:
1 . The authors proposed PROXGEN for stochastic proximal gradient descent with non-convex non-smooth regularizers and preconditioners. Compared with previous works, the major improvement in this paper is the extension to enable positive preconditioners.

2 . The authors show that the proposed PROXGEN algorithm enjoys the same convergence rate as stochastic proximal gradient descent without preconditioners. It would be best if the authors could show the advantage of using preconditioners in PROXGEN compared with previous works in the convergence rate.

3 . Previous studies have shown that there exists a non-convergence issue in the standard Adam algorithm.

"On the convergence of adam and beyond." ICLR (2019).

Essentially without using an extra max step for the preconditioner part, Adam may diverge in certain cases. Here the author directly extend stochastic proximal gradient descent on to Adam and showed its convergence, the authors might want to show the readers why such a non-convergence issue does not exist in the proximal setting.

4 . The following work shows that unifying SGD and AMSGrad(Adam) lead to better result with convergence guarantees in the nonconvex setting

"Closing the generalization gap of adaptive gradient methods in training deep neural networks." IJCAI (2020).

Also the following work shows a tight convergence rate for the adaptive gradient method in the nonconvex setting.  

"On the convergence of adaptive gradient methods for nonconvex optimization." arXiv preprint arXiv:1808.05671 (2018).

The authors might also want to comment on these works.
content.confidence: 4: The reviewer is confident but not absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct

content.title: Response to Reviewer 3
content.comment:
Dear Reviewer 3,

Thank you for your constructive feedback.

[Q1: The advantage of using preconditioners in ProxGen]

Please see the global response.

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[Q2: Previous studies have shown that there exists a non-convergence issue in the standard Adam. The authors might want to show the readers why such a non-convergence issue does not exist in the proximal setting.]

For the convergence analysis of Adam, the positiveness of the quantity $\Gamma_t = \frac{\sqrt{V_t}}{\alpha_t} - \frac{\sqrt{V_{t-1}}}{\alpha_{t-1}}$ (the changes of effective learning rate) does matter in the proof. The max step is inevitable to make this quantity $\Gamma_t$ always positive [1]. However, all these arguments were made in the context of convex optimization (i.e, convex regret bound). 

On the other hand, the proof for our Theorem 1 does not depend on the quantity $\Gamma_t$ under the Lipschitz continuous gradient. Instead, the condition (C-4) is required to handle the preconditioners in our formulation, which is a mild assumption as we discussed (see remarks in Section 3).

In fact, such a non-convergence issue might not exist even in the non-proximal settings. Under the Lipschitz continuous gradient, it is known that Adam converges to a stationary point with the same convergence rate as vanilla SGD [2,3], whose proofs also do not depend on the quantity $\Gamma_t$.

Moreover, our Theorem 1 with an empty regularizer (i.e., $\mathcal{R}(\cdot) = 0$) can recover the same convergence rates in [2,3].

[1] On the Convergence of Adam and Beyond, Reddi et al., ICLR 2018.

[2] Adaptive Methods for Non-convex Optimization, Zaheer et al., NeurIPS 2018.

[3] On the Convergence of a Class of Adam-type Algorithms in Non-convex Optimization,. Chen et al., ICLR 2019. 

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[Q3: The authors might also want to comment on these works.]

Thank you for letting us know those references. We will include those references in later revision.

content.title: An incremental algorithmic paper without strong motivation
content.review:
Summary. This paper proposes a unified framework for stochastic proximal gradient descent called ProxGen, which introduces both momentum and preconditioner to stochastic proximal gradient descent. Furthermore, it can cover a broad range of stochastic gradient descent algorithms. Under this framework, the authors give a convergence analysis of stochastic proximal gradient descent for both nonconvex loss and nonconvex regularizer.  Moreover, they apply ProxGen to training sparse or binary neural networks with promising results. 

Overall. I think their proposed framework is interesting with the solid theoretical analysis. However, their motivation is not clear enough, and the application of ProxGen is narrow in their work. Thus I think this work should not be accepted to ICLR in the current version. 
- Although able to give a theoretical analysis of stochastic proximal gradient descent with both preconditioner and momentum, the benefit of introducing preconditioner is not supported in theoretical analysis, as the convergence bound is the same $\mathcal{O}(\frac{1}{\epsilon^4})$ compared with previous works (e.g., Davis et al. 2020). 
- The introduction of nonconvex regularizers needs more motivation. Empirical results of nonconvex regularizer compared with convex ones (e.g., $\ell_1$ regularizer) is not supportive enough either. 
- Their application is too narrow (only limited to sparse and binary neural network training),  which does not agree with their title ``for deep learning''. 

Main concerns. 
- The introduction of preconditioners to stochastic proximal gradient descent is not well motivated. While the author highlights the difficulties of analyzing the convergence of stochastic proximal gradient descent with preconditioners, such modification's benefits are not clear in their theoretical analysis. Although the authors have demonstrated the superiority of ProxGen in experiments, it would be better to analyze the impact of preconditioners in the theoretical analysis (I think it should affect the constant in convergence rate). 
- The proposed nonconvex regularizer also lacks enough motivation, and the empirical results seem not very supportive. Although the authors claim that nonconvex regularizer can be more effective than convex ones, 
the experiment results in Table 3 indicate the opposite result: $\ell_1$ regularizer works better than other regularizers except on ResNet-32 (where the performance is very close). The experiment results in Fig 2, 3, 6, and 7 also seems to have the same trend, and perhaps the authors should find some other applications that are especially suitable in deep learning for nonconvex regularizers. 
- The authors only apply ProxGen to training the sparse and binary neural network, which seems too narrow considering ``for deep learning'' in their title. Perhaps the authors can add more deep learning applications that involve (possibly nonconvex) regularizers in the objective, or it would be better to change the paper to focus more on sparse or binary neural network training. 

Minor issues.
- The theoretical analysis seems unable to cover neural networks with batch normalization (BN) or dropout (DO). Moreover, the authors also do not indicate whether they use BN or DO in their experiment details. 
Since the use of BN and DO can significantly affect neural networks' performance, the authors should add those experiment settings in the appendix. 
- The experimental results in Figures 2 and 3 (also in Figures 6 and 7) are not easy to understand. Specifically, when I try to compare different regularizers' performance, I found it very difficult to read across different subfigures (and even with different scales in the y-axis). Perhaps the authors can find a better way to present these results.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 1
content.comment:
Dear Reviewer 1,

Thank you for your constructive feedback.

[Q1: The benefit of preconditioners is not clear in theoretical analysis.]

Please see the general response above.

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[Q2: The proposed non-convex regularizer lacks enough motivation, and the empirical results are not supportive. Perhaps the authors should find some other applications.]

We mean that our ProxGen shows much better performance than subgradient counterparts when considering non-convex regularizers (for example, Figure 2-(b,c,d), Figure 3-(b,c,d)), but there is no significant difference when considering convex regularizers as in Figure 2-(a) or Figure 3-(a). In this sense, ProxGen with non-convex regularizers is more effective than with convex regularizers.

The third contribution point in the introduction seems a bit confusing, so we will modify this in the revision.

Per the reviewer’s suggestion, we plan to add other applications in deep learning in future work.

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[Q3: The theoretical analysis seems unable to cover neural networks with batch normalization (BN) and Dropout (DO). Since the use of BN and DO can significantly affect neural networks’ performance, the authors should add those experiment settings in the Appendix.]

In this work, our goal is to present a unified understanding in standard non-convex optimization settings, but per your suggestion, considering BN and DO layers in theory would be interesting for future directions. In terms of experiments, VGG-like networks already have both BN and DO layers and our ProxGen also works well for those layers as in Figure 2. 

Per your suggestion, we will include more experiments on BN and DO layers in revisions.

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------


[Q4: The experimental results in Figure 2 and 3 (also 6 and 7) are not easy to understand for comparing different regularizers’ performance.]

We are sorry for the inconvenience. For ease of comparison among regularizers, we will match the scale of y-axis in Figure 2 and 3 in later revision. Thank you for your suggestions.

content.title: General Response to Reviewers
content.comment:
Thank you for your constructive feedback to all reviewers.

We answer here the common question: "the benefit of preconditioners in ProxGen in terms of theory"

Since the derived convergence rate (known as optimal) is the same for both vanilla SGD and preconditioned gradient descent, we provide the advantages of preconditioners in a different perspective.

In our Theorem 1 and Corollary 1, the constants $Q_1, Q_2$ and $Q_3$ are all proportional to the $1/\gamma$ according to our proofs where the constant $\gamma$ is defined in our condition (C-4). As you can see, the convergence rate depends on this constant and the benefit of preconditioners can be found here.

To view this more clearly, we consider the diagonal matrix adaptation of AdaGrad [1], i.e., $\alpha_t = \alpha$ and $C_t = \sqrt{\sum_{\tau=1}^{t} g_\tau \odot g_\tau}$, with the total iteration T. 

In this setting, the $1/\gamma$ can be computed as 

$\frac{1}{\alpha} \times \max_{i=1,2,\cdots,d} ||g_{1:T, i}||_2$ 

where the vector $g_{1:T, i} = [g_{1,i}, g_{2,i}, \cdots, g_{T,i}]$ is a collection of all gradient history for the i-th coordinate. We can see the advantages of adaptive methods (i.e., using preconditioners) since $1/\gamma$ could be smaller **when the gradient is sparse (the data features are sparse)**. This coincides with the convex regret theory in AdaGrad (Duchi et al., 2011), which also holds in our theory even with non-convex smooth loss and non-convex regularizers. This argument can be similarly applied to Adam.

We will include this discussion in remarks after Corollary 1 at Section 3 in the revision.

[1] Adaptive Subgradient Methods for Online Learning and Stochastic Optimization, Duchi et al., 2011.
